For example, input 55 (row 1, col 1, ch 0) has values like `-0.694 -1.615 -1.207 ... 2.697 ... -2.474`; input 105 (row 2, col 1, ch 0) has `0.563 -3.588 ... 2.245 ... -2.085`. This looks like a vertical position map for an object confined to the left edge.  
- Channel 1 has large weights for columns 2–8, rows 1–8. For example, input 61 (row 1, col 2, ch 1) has `-1.683 -3.169 2.039 ... -2.772 ... 2.062`; input 91 (row 1, col 8, ch 1) also has large structured values. This looks like a spatial map for an object that can move throughout the rest of the playable area.  
- Channel 4 has large weights across all playable cells (rows 1–8, cols 1–8). For example, input 64 (row 1, col 2, ch 4) has `-1.184 ... 1.018 ... -1.381`; input 109 (row 2, col 1, ch 4) is similarly large. This is consistent with a background/empty-cell channel.  
- Channels 2 and 3 show only moderate weights, mostly around the border, suggesting static walls rather than dynamic objects.  

The output layer also supports a vertical-control game. The output biases are `b3 = [0.931, 1.261, 1.065, 0.861, 0.855]`, so up/down are favored over left/right/no-op. Many W3 rows have much larger weights for up/down than for left/right, e.g. row 3: `0.133 1.003 1.898 0.059 0.046`, and row 17: `-0.056 1.178 1.165 -0.032 -0.068`. Left/right weights are often close to each other and to no-op, indicating they are largely irrelevant.

Reasoning: The weights imply two moving entities: one restricted to column 1 (the left edge) and one moving in columns 2–8. The remaining playable cells are covered by a background channel. This is exactly the structure of a Pong-like game: a paddle on the left moves vertically, and a ball travels in the rest of the grid. The action space is 5-way, but only up/down matter for the paddle; left/right are effectively unused. Games like Snake, Pac-Man, or Maze would have different object distributions—e.g. a snake body spanning many cells, multiple ghosts, or a single goal cell—not this left-edge paddle plus free-moving ball pattern. The strong up/down bias in the output layer further rules out games requiring four-directional movement.

Game: Pong (single-player variant, controlling the left paddle).
